extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in media, satire, free-speech debates, and Muslim communities (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether satirical cartoons (especially those targeting religion/minorities) function as legitimate humour or as acts that reproduce domination, vilification, and historical prejudice. Focuses on intent, effect, historical genealogy, and power dynamics rather than only free-speech claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech as affirmation of domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether reprinting/producing the cartoons is 'about using speech to reaffirm domination' rather than a neutral exercise of free speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues: 'Reprinting the Charlie Hebdo cartoons is not about free speech. It is about using speech to reaffirm domination.' Evaluate whether the speech serves to demonstrate or reproduce hierarchical relations (dominant over marginalised) rather than to critique or entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and ideological genealogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the depiction continues a long-standing historical lineage of vilifying the target (here, depictions of the prophet/Islam) rather than being a new, isolated act of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the piece notes, reducing the cartoons to free-speech issues 'obscures their historical and ideological genealogy.' Consider medieval and Enlightenment portrayals (Antichrist, devil, 'robber', 'enemy of reason') and whether the cartoon repeats entrenched tropes rooted in centuries of vilification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement of existing stereotypes (not satirical critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the cartoon challenges power or merely 'recycles' and reinforces stereotypes (e.g., portraying Muslims as 'born terrorists-in-the-making').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks, 'what is satirical about these, when Muslims are already viewed as born terrorists-in-the-making?' If the work simply reiterates dominant negative tropes rather than subverting them, it should not be treated as meaningful satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivialisation of real harms (e.g., terrorism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the humour treats serious harms — such as terrorism or suicide bombing — lightly or as a source of amusement, thereby normalising or trivialising suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece states, 'it is difficult to see how anyone ... could find a cartoon of the prophet as a terrorist/suicide bomber amusing without also treating terrorism itself lightly.' If the depiction makes light of violence in a way that desensitises or normalises it, that is a negative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional provocation to elicit predictable backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether creators use provocative vilification knowing it will 'goad' some into violent response and then exploit that response politically or culturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that the 'Muslim-baiting intelligentsia relies on precisely its own vilifications to incite the violence which it then feigns to be horrified and surprised by.' Assess foreseeability of backlash and whether the provocation is instrumentalised to justify further negative portrayals of the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as spectacle of mastery / display of dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the depiction functions as a public 'spectacle of mastery' that demonstrates the dominant group's control or the target group's abasement, rather than serving artistic or critical aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing Saidiya Hartman, the author suggests derogatory caricatures can be 'spectacles of mastery' used to 'establish dominion.' Look for signs that the work's purpose is to display superiority (public amusement, demonstrations of dominion) rather than to foster critique or dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish condemnation of violence from endorsement of defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether critics and defenders appropriately condemn violent reactions while simultaneously holding creators accountable for defamation and vilification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states it should be possible 'to condemn violence by Muslims without giving a free pass to those who defame and vilify their religion.' Good evaluation separates legitimate critique of violence from excusing defamatory speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of freedom being invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine what version of 'freedom' is being defended — whether it is used to protect dissent/critique or to shield acts that reproduce domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns 'defending domination in the name of freedom just confirms that not all conceptions of freedom are equally worth defending.' Scrutinise whether appeals to free speech are masking power assertions that harm marginalised groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual sensitivity to target's marginalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the social position and vulnerability of the target group: does the cartoon further marginalise an already vulnerable community?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes condemnation is aimed at 'the use of speech to dominate and degrade the already marginal or vulnerable.' Evaluate impact on an already marginalised community and whether the piece amplifies their marginalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secularisation of religious vilification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether portrayals are a secularised continuation of earlier religious demonisations (e.g., Antichrist -> terrorist) and thus maintain the same exclusionary function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues the 'cartoons of the prophet as a terrorist' are a 'secularisation of the figure of the Antichrist.' Check whether contemporary secular tropes are functionally equivalent to older religious demonisations and serve the same othering purpose.
